title: Why the Midwives Lied to Pharaoh to Save Hebrew Babies
paragraphs: Why the Midwives Lied to Pharaoh to Save Hebrew Babies
There are moments in Scripture that make people uncomfortable.
Moments where the Bible does not fit neatly inside religious systems.
Moments where survival, courage, terror, obedience, and moral tension collide in the dark.
This is one of those moments.
Two women stood between a murderous king and helpless newborn babies.
And they lied.
Not for money.
Not for selfish ambition.
Not for manipulation.
They lied because babies were about to be slaughtered.
And heaven saw everything.

Most people read Exodus quickly and miss the emotional weight buried inside the text. But if you slow down long enough to feel the terror of what was happening in Egypt, this story becomes devastatingly real.
This was not merely political oppression.
This was attempted extermination.
This was state-sponsored genocide against covenant children.
This was demonic fear trying to destroy the future before it could be born.
And strangely enough… the first recorded human heroes in the book of Exodus are not warriors.
Not prophets.
Not kings.
Not priests.
Midwives.
Women whose hands caught fragile babies while death waited outside.
Exodus 1:15–17 says:

“Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah; and he said, ‘When you are helping the Hebrew women to give birth and see them upon the birthstool, if it is a son, then you shall put him to death; but if it is a daughter, then she shall live.’ But the midwives feared God, and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them, but let the boys live.”
The Hebrew phrase used here is:
וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים
“Vattirena hamyalledot et-haElohim”
“The midwives feared God.”
This changes everything.
The text does not first emphasize political rebellion.
It emphasizes fear of God.
The Hebrew word used for “feared” is יָרֵא (yare’).
This word means reverence, awe, trembling obedience, deep recognition of divine authority.
Their fear of God overpowered their fear of Pharaoh.
And that matters because Pharaoh was not merely a ruler.
In Egypt, Pharaoh was viewed as divine.
To disobey him was dangerous.
To oppose him could cost your life.
But these women understood something modern culture desperately needs to rediscover:
Earthly authority is never ultimate authority.
When human governments command evil, obedience to God becomes higher.
That is exactly why this passage has echoed through generations of persecuted believers.
Because sometimes righteousness is costly.
Sometimes doing what is holy puts you in danger.
Sometimes faithfulness requires courage while your hands shake.
And the terrifying part?
The midwives had no guarantee God would rescue them.
We read this story knowing the ending.
They did not.
Imagine the emotional tension.
Every Hebrew mother screaming in labor.
Every newborn son wrapped in cloth.
Every knock at the door potentially carrying death.
Every heartbeat filled with fear.
And still… these women chose life.
The names Shiphrah and Puah matter more than most readers realize.
Pharaoh’s personal name is not even mentioned in Exodus 1.
But God preserved the names of the midwives forever.
Think about that.
Empires collapse.
Tyrants rot.
But heaven remembers ordinary people who protect life.
Shiphrah likely comes from a Hebrew root associated with beauty or brightness.
Puah may carry ideas connected to crying out or splendor.
These women became beautiful in the eyes of God because they protected what evil wanted destroyed.
Then comes the moment that creates theological tension.
Exodus 1:18–19:

“So the king of Egypt called for the midwives and said to them, ‘Why have you done this thing, and let the boys live?’ The midwives said to Pharaoh, ‘Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife can get to them.’”
This was not the whole truth.
And many people wrestle with this.
Did God approve of lying?
Was deception justified?
Why does Scripture appear to honor them afterward?
The answer requires careful biblical understanding.
The Bible does not explicitly praise the lie itself.
It praises their fear of God and their protection of innocent life.
Exodus 1:20–21 says:
“So God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became very mighty. Because the midwives feared God, He established households for them.”
Notice the repeated emphasis.
“Because the midwives feared God.”
Not:
“Because they lied skillfully.”
The text centers on covenant loyalty to God over participation in murder.
This distinction matters deeply.
Scripture consistently condemns false witness, deception for evil, manipulation, and dishonest gain.
Yet Scripture also recognizes moments where protecting innocent life under evil oppression creates morally tragic circumstances.
This is why many theologians compare this event to Rahab in Joshua 2.
Rahab hid the Israelite spies and misled the authorities searching for them.
Hebrews 11:31 later honors her faith.
James 2:25 highlights her actions flowing from faith.
Again, the emphasis is covenant loyalty and protection of life under wicked tyranny.
This does not create a universal permission slip for lying.
The Bible never teaches situational ethics where truth becomes meaningless.
Instead, these passages reveal the horror of living in a fallen world where evil regimes force people into impossible situations.
The moral burden in Exodus falls primarily on Pharaoh.
He was commanding infanticide.
He was weaponizing authority against babies.
And the midwives refused to become instruments of death.
This is one reason the story still grips people emotionally thousands of years later.
Because deep down, we recognize the weight of moral courage.
Most people imagine they would resist evil if history demanded it.
But reality is terrifying.
People lose jobs.
Families get threatened.
Reputations get destroyed.
Fear silences entire populations.
Yet these women stood in the gap.
Not with armies.
With conviction.
And if we are honest, this story exposes something painful inside many of us.
How often do we stay silent because speaking truth feels costly?
How often do we compromise because fear feels stronger than conviction?
How often do we protect comfort more than righteousness?
The midwives remind us that courage is rarely loud.
Sometimes courage looks like quietly refusing to participate in evil.
Sometimes holiness looks like protecting the vulnerable when nobody applauds.
Sometimes faithfulness happens behind closed doors where only God sees.
And there is something even deeper happening spiritually in Exodus.
Pharaoh was trying to kill Hebrew sons.
Centuries later, Herod would try to kill Hebrew sons again after hearing about the birth of Jesus.
Matthew 2 echoes Exodus intentionally.
Satan repeatedly targets covenant seed.
Why?
Because redemption was coming through a child.
The enemy often attacks what carries future deliverance.
That is why this story feels spiritually alive even now.
Some people reading this have spent years feeling like hell itself was trying to destroy them before they could become who God called them to be.
Some survived childhood trauma.
Abuse.
Addiction.
Depression.
Violence.
Rejection.
Suicidal thoughts.
And you still do not fully realize that your survival may itself be evidence of divine purpose.
The Hebrew babies Pharaoh wanted dead included Moses.
Imagine if the midwives had surrendered.
Imagine if fear won.
Imagine if they obeyed evil authority instead of God.
A deliverer would have died in infancy.
One act of courage can alter history.
One refusal to participate in evil can preserve generations.
One moment of fearing God more than man can become part of redemption itself.
That is why this passage cannot be reduced to shallow arguments online.
This is about the cost of righteousness in dark times.
And there is another detail many overlook.
The Hebrew word for midwives is מְיַלְּדֹת (meyalledot).
Its root relates to bringing forth birth.
These women were literally called to help life emerge.
Pharaoh commanded them to reverse their calling.
To turn deliverers of life into agents of death.
That is exactly how evil works.
Sin always tries to corrupt God-given purpose.
It tries to make protectors become predators.
It tries to make shepherds become wolves.
It tries to make truth-bearers become liars.
It tries to make image-bearers forget God.
But the midwives resisted corruption.
And because of that, their names still breathe through history.
There is also powerful theological significance in the phrase “let the boys live.”
The Hebrew says:
וַתְּחַיֶּיןָ אֶת־הַיְלָדִים
“Vattechayyena et-hayeladim”
“They caused the children to live.”
The root here is חָיָה (chayah), meaning “to live,” “to preserve alive,” “to revive.”
This same life-language echoes throughout Scripture.
God is repeatedly portrayed as the giver and sustainer of life.
The midwives aligned themselves with the life-giving heart of God instead of the death-producing agenda of Pharaoh.
That does not mean they were sinless.
It means they chose righteousness over participation in murder.
And perhaps that is part of what makes this story so emotionally overwhelming.
God works through flawed humans.
Not perfect humans.
Real humans.
Terrified humans.
Complicated humans.
Humans forced into difficult moments inside a fallen world.
Some readers struggle because they want every biblical situation reduced into simplistic formulas.
But Scripture often gives us reality instead.
Messy.
Painful.
Complex.
Human.
And through it all, God’s sovereignty remains intact.
The story also confronts modern believers with uncomfortable questions.
Would we protect the vulnerable if it endangered us?
Would we obey God if culture mocked us?
Would we stand against evil if the cost became personal?
Or have we become so addicted to comfort that conviction disappears under pressure?
This is why Exodus still cuts deep.
Because Pharaoh is not merely an ancient king.
Pharaoh represents every system that exalts itself against God.
Every power structure demanding compromise.
Every voice pressuring people to participate in evil for the sake of convenience, safety, acceptance, or survival.
And the midwives remind us that sometimes the holiest people in history are invisible to the world.
No stage.
No platform.
No empire.
Just courage.
Quiet courage.
Holy courage.
The kind of courage heaven never forgets.
There are people reading this who feel insignificant.
You think your obedience does not matter.
You think your quiet faithfulness goes unseen.
But Scripture says otherwise.
God recorded the names of two midwives forever.
Not because they were powerful.
Because they feared Him.
And maybe someone reading this right now has been compromising truth because fear has controlled your life.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of conflict.
Fear of losing people.
Fear of standing alone.
Fear of consequences.
But eventually every believer faces the same question the midwives faced:
Who do you fear more?
God?
Or Pharaoh?
That question still divides humanity.
Jesus Himself later said in Matthew 10:28:
“Do not fear those who kill the body but are unable to kill the soul; but rather fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.”
The Greek word for fear there is φοβέω (phobeó).
It carries the same deep reverential seriousness seen in the Hebrew concept of fearing God.
Biblical fear of God is not terror that pushes us away from Him.
It is awe that brings us under His authority.
The midwives understood this long before Sinai.
Long before the Law was formally given.
They recognized that innocent life mattered to God.
And their actions became part of preserving the line through which redemption history unfolded.
Moses survived.
Israel survived.
The covenant continued.
And ultimately, centuries later, Jesus Christ entered the world through that preserved covenant people.
This story points beyond itself.
It whispers about a greater Deliverer.
Because every rescued Hebrew child in Exodus foreshadows the God who rescues sinners from death.
Jesus did not come merely to improve behavior.
He came to rescue people enslaved under sin.
The same way Israel groaned under Pharaoh, humanity groans under bondage.
And Christ entered history to confront the kingdom of darkness itself.
That is why the Gospel matters.
Because every human eventually discovers that evil is not only outside us.
It is inside us too.
We have all lied.
Compromised.
Failed.
Broken trust.
Disobeyed God.
Fallen short.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
The Greek phrase “fall short” is ὑστεροῦνται (hysterountai).
It carries the sense of lacking, failing to attain, coming behind.
Humanity cannot save itself through morality.
Not even heroic moments erase sin.
That is why we need grace.
The beauty of the Gospel is not that humans are flawless.
The beauty of the Gospel is that Jesus saves flawed people.
People like Moses.
People like Rahab.
People like David.
People like Peter.
People like us.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the overwhelming mercy of God.
Christ absorbed judgment so repentant sinners could receive forgiveness.
And maybe that is why this story lingers emotionally.
Because it reminds us that evil is real.
Fear is real.
Oppression is real.
But courage through faith is real too.
And God still sees those who choose righteousness when darkness grows loud.
Somebody needed this reminder today.
Your obedience matters.
Your refusal to compromise matters.
Your quiet faithfulness matters.
Your stand for truth matters.
And heaven notices what the world ignores.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than most people expected.
Sometimes the people who save generations are the ones history almost forgot.
Filipino Version:
Bakit Nagsinungaling ang mga Hilot kay Paraon Para Iligtas ang mga Sanggol na Hebreo
May mga bahagi sa Biblia na hindi komportable basahin.
Mga sandaling hindi kasya sa mabababaw na sermon.
Mga tagpong bumabangga ang takot, pananampalataya, buhay, kamatayan, kapangyarihan, at konsensya.
Ito ang isa sa mga iyon.
Dalawang babae ang tumayo sa pagitan ng isang mamamatay-taong hari at mga bagong silang na sanggol.
At nagsinungaling sila.
Hindi dahil gahaman sila.
Hindi dahil gusto nilang manloko.
Hindi dahil rebelde sila.
Nagsinungaling sila dahil may mga sanggol na malapit nang patayin.
At nakita iyon ng langit.
Karamihan sa mga tao mabilis basahin ang Exodo at hindi nararamdaman ang bigat ng nangyayari.
Pero kapag hinayaan mong lumubog ang puso mo sa takot ng panahong iyon… maiintindihan mo kung gaano ito kabigat.
Hindi ito simpleng pang-aapi.
Ito ay pagtatangkang lipulin ang isang buong lahi.
Ito ay sistematikong pagpatay sa mga anak ng tipan.
Ito ay takot ng kadiliman sa hinaharap na hindi pa ipinapanganak.
At nakakagulat… ang unang mga bayani sa aklat ng Exodo ay hindi hari.
Hindi propeta.
Hindi mandirigma.
Hindi pari.
Mga hilot.
Mga babaeng ang mga kamay ay humahawak ng bagong buhay habang naghihintay ang kamatayan sa labas.
Sinasabi sa Exodo 1:15–17:

“Then the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah; and he said, ‘When you are helping the Hebrew women to give birth and see them upon the birthstool, if it is a son, then you shall put him to death; but if it is a daughter, then she shall live.’ But the midwives feared God, and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them, but let the boys live.”
Ang ginamit na salitang Hebreo ay:
וַתִּירֶאןָ הַמְיַלְּדֹת אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים
“Vattirena hamyalledot et-haElohim”
“Natakot ang mga hilot sa Diyos.”
At dito nagbabago ang lahat.
Hindi unang binigyang-diin ng Kasulatan ang pagrerebelde nila.
Ang binigyang-diin ay ang kanilang takot sa Diyos.
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “takot” ay יָרֵא (yare’).
Hindi lang ito simpleng takot.
Ito ay banal na paggalang.
Pagkamangha.
Panginginig sa harap ng awtoridad ng Diyos.
Mas malakas ang takot nila sa Diyos kaysa takot nila kay Paraon.
At mahalagang maunawaan iyon.
Si Paraon ay hindi lang hari.
Sa Egypto, itinuturing siyang parang diyos.
Ang pagsuway sa kanya ay maaaring ikamatay mo.
Pero naunawaan ng mga hilot ang isang katotohanang kailangan muling marinig ng mundo ngayon:
Ang kapangyarihan ng tao ay hindi kailanman mas mataas kaysa kapangyarihan ng Diyos.
Kapag inuutos ng tao ang kasamaan, mas mataas pa rin ang pagsunod sa Diyos.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit napakalakas ng kuwentong ito kahit libo-libong taon na ang lumipas.
Dahil minsan mahal ang pagiging matuwid.
Minsan mapanganib ang paggawa ng tama.
Minsan nanginginig ka habang pinipili mong sumunod sa Diyos.
At ang nakakatakot?
Walang kasiguraduhan ang mga hilot na ililigtas sila ng Diyos.
Alam natin ang ending ng kuwento.
Sila, hindi.
Isipin mo ang tensyon.
Bawat inang Hebreo na sumisigaw sa panganganak.
Bawat sanggol na lalaki na iniluluwal.
Bawat katok sa pinto na maaaring may dalang kamatayan.
At sa kabila ng lahat… pinili pa rin nilang protektahan ang buhay.
Napakahalaga ng mga pangalang Shiphrah at Puah.
Ang pangalan ni Paraon mismo ay hindi binanggit sa Exodo 1.
Pero ang pangalan ng mga hilot… isinulat ng Diyos magpakailanman.
Pag-isipan mo iyon.
Nawawala ang mga imperyo.
Nabubulok ang mga diktador.
Pero hindi nakakalimutan ng langit ang mga ordinaryong taong nagprotekta ng buhay.
Pagkatapos nito dumating ang bahagi na madalas pagdebatehan.

“So the king of Egypt called for the midwives and said to them, ‘Why have you done this thing, and let the boys live?’ The midwives said to Pharaoh, ‘Because the Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women; for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife can get to them.’”
Hindi iyon buong katotohanan.
Kaya maraming nagtatanong:
Pinuri ba ng Diyos ang pagsisinungaling?
Pinapayagan ba ng Biblia ang panlilinlang?
Bakit tila pinagpala pa sila pagkatapos?
Mahalagang maging maingat dito.
Hindi pinuri ng Diyos ang kasinungalingan mismo.
Ang pinuri ng Diyos ay ang kanilang takot sa Kanya at ang kanilang pagtangging makibahagi sa pagpatay ng inosente.
“So God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became very mighty. Because the midwives feared God, He established households for them.”
Pansinin mo.
Paulit-ulit ang diin:
“Because the midwives feared God.”
Hindi sinabi:
“Because they lied well.”
Napakahalaga ng pagkakaibang iyon.
Hindi kailanman itinuro ng Biblia na okay lang magsinungaling para sa pansariling interes.
Kinokondena ng Kasulatan ang maling saksi, panlilinlang, at kasinungalingang nagdudulot ng kasamaan.
Pero ipinapakita rin ng Biblia ang bigat ng pamumuhay sa isang makasalanang mundo kung saan may mga pagkakataong pinipilit ng masasamang sistema ang tao sa napakahirap na sitwasyon.
Ang tunay na kasamaan sa kuwento ay si Paraon.
Siya ang nag-utos ng pagpatay sa mga sanggol.
Siya ang gumamit ng kapangyarihan laban sa mga inosente.
At tumanggi ang mga hilot na maging instrumento ng kamatayan.
Ito ang dahilan kung bakit hanggang ngayon tumatama ito sa puso ng tao.
Dahil lahat tayo may sandaling kailangang pumili.
Mananahimik ba tayo dahil natatakot tayo?
O maninindigan tayo kahit may kapalit?
Madalas iniisip ng mga tao na magiging matapang sila kapag dumating ang kasamaan.
Pero ang totoo… nakakatakot.
May nawawalan ng trabaho.
May tinatakwil.
May pinapatahimik.
May inuusig.
Pero tumayo pa rin ang mga hilot.
Hindi gamit ang espada.
Kundi gamit ang paninindigan.
At kung magiging tapat tayo sa sarili natin, may inilalantad itong masakit.
Ilang beses na tayong nanahimik dahil mas mahalaga ang comfort kaysa katotohanan?
Ilang beses na tayong natakot mawalan ng tao kaya nagkompromiso tayo?
Ilang beses nating pinili ang seguridad kaysa pagsunod sa Diyos?
Ipinapaalala ng mga hilot na hindi laging maingay ang tapang.
Minsan tahimik lang itong pagtanggi na makibahagi sa mali.
Minsan kabanalan ang simpleng pagprotekta sa mahina kahit walang nakakakita.
At may mas malalim pang nangyayari rito.
Sinubukang patayin ni Paraon ang mga anak na lalaki ng Israel.
Pagkalipas ng maraming siglo, sinubukan ding patayin ni Herodes ang mga batang lalaki matapos marinig ang kapanganakan ni Jesus.
Sinasalamin ng Mateo 2 ang Exodo.
Paulit-ulit tinatarget ng kadiliman ang binhing may dalang pagtubos.
Bakit?
Dahil may darating na Tagapagligtas.
At madalas sinusubukan ng kaaway patayin ang layunin bago pa ito lumago.
May mga taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na pakiramdam nila buong buhay silang nilalabanan ng kadiliman.
Trauma.
Abuso.
Depresyon.
Pagkagumon.
Pagpapakamatay na isipin.
Pagkawasak.
At baka hindi mo pa rin lubos nauunawaan na maaaring dahilan kung bakit ka nabuhay ay dahil may layunin ang Diyos para sa iyo.
Kasama sa mga sanggol na gustong patayin ni Paraon si Moises.
Isipin mo kung sumuko ang mga hilot.
Isipin mo kung nanaig ang takot.
Maaaring namatay ang isang magiging tagapagligtas habang sanggol pa.
Minsan isang matapang na desisyon lang ang kayang baguhin ang kasaysayan.
Isang pagtanggi sa kasamaan.
Isang tao na mas natakot sa Diyos kaysa sa tao.
At may isa pang detalye na madalas hindi napapansin.
Ang salitang Hebreo para sa “mga hilot” ay מְיַלְּדֹת (meyalledot).
Nagmula ito sa ugat na may kaugnayan sa pagdadala ng buhay.
Ang calling nila ay tumulong magluwal ng buhay.
Pero gusto ni Paraon na gamitin sila para magdala ng kamatayan.
Ganiyan gumalaw ang kasamaan.
Sinisira nito ang orihinal na layunin ng Diyos.
Ginagawang mandaragit ang tagapangalaga.
Ginagawang manhid ang konsensya.
Ginagawang normal ang kasamaan.
Pero tumanggi ang mga hilot.
At dahil doon, buhay pa rin ang pangalan nila hanggang ngayon.
Sinasabi rin sa Exodo:
וַתְּחַיֶּיןָ אֶת־הַיְלָדִים
“Vattechayyena et-hayeladim”
“Pinanatili nilang buhay ang mga bata.”
Ang ugat ng salitang ito ay חָיָה (chayah).
Ibig sabihin: mabuhay, panatilihing buhay, magbigay-buhay.
Ang Diyos ay Diyos ng buhay.
At pinili ng mga hilot ang panig ng buhay kaysa kamatayan.
Hindi ibig sabihin nito perpekto sila.
Ibig sabihin pinili nilang huwag makibahagi sa pagpatay.
At marahil iyon ang dahilan kung bakit napakalalim ng kuwentong ito.
Ginagamit ng Diyos ang mga totoong tao.
Hindi perpektong tao.
Takot na tao.
Sugatang tao.
Komplikadong tao.
Mga taong sinusubukang sumunod sa Diyos sa gitna ng magulong mundo.
At may tanong ang kuwentong ito para sa ating lahat.
Kapag dumating ang pressure… sino ang mas katatakutan mo?
Ang Diyos?
O si Paraon?
Iyan pa rin ang tanong hanggang ngayon.
Sinabi ni Jesus sa Mateo 10:28:
“Do not fear those who kill the body but are unable to kill the soul; but rather fear Him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “fear” ay φοβέω (phobeó).
Hindi lang ito panic.
Ito ay malalim na paggalang at pagkilala sa kapangyarihan ng Diyos.
Naunawaan iyon ng mga hilot bago pa man ibigay ang Kautusan sa Sinai.
Naunawaan nila na mahalaga sa Diyos ang inosenteng buhay.
At dahil sa kanilang katapangan… nabuhay si Moises.
Nabuhay ang Israel.
Nagpatuloy ang tipan.
At paglipas ng maraming siglo… dumating si Jesucristo mula sa bayang iyon.
At dito lalong lumalalim ang kuwento.
Dahil hindi lang ito tungkol sa dalawang hilot.
Ito ay anino ng mas dakilang pagliligtas.
Gaya ng pagliligtas ng Diyos sa mga sanggol mula sa kamatayan, inililigtas din Niya ang mga makasalanan mula sa espirituwal na kamatayan.
Tayong lahat ay nagkasala.
Lahat tayo bumagsak.
Lahat tayo may kasinungalingan.
May kompromiso.
May sugat.
Romans 3:23:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.”
Ang salitang Griyego para sa “fall short” ay ὑστεροῦνται (hysterountai).
Ibig sabihin kulang.
Hindi sapat.
Hindi maabot ang pamantayan ng kabanalan ng Diyos.
Hindi kayang iligtas ng tao ang sarili niya.
Kaya kailangan natin si Cristo.
Ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo ay hindi dahil perpekto ang tao.
Ang kagandahan ng Ebanghelyo ay inililigtas ni Jesus ang mga hindi perpekto.
Mga taong tulad ni Moises.
Tulad ni Rahab.
Tulad ni Pedro.
Tulad natin.
Sa krus nakita natin kung gaano kaseryoso ang kasalanan.
Pero nakita rin natin kung gaano kalalim ang awa ng Diyos.
Inako ni Cristo ang hatol para makaranas tayo ng kapatawaran.
At baka may taong nagbabasa nito ngayon na pagod na.
Takot na.
Tahimik na lumalaban.
Ito ang paalala mo:
Nakikita ng Diyos ang katapatan na hindi napapansin ng mundo.
Nakikita Niya ang tahimik mong paninindigan.
Nakikita Niya ang laban na hindi alam ng iba.
At hindi nasasayang ang pagsunod sa Diyos.
Maging tapat.
Mas malalim itong tumama kaysa inaasahan mo.
Minsan ang mga taong nagligtas ng mga henerasyon ay iyong mga halos nakalimutan ng kasaysayan.
